summary: Extends ACME so certificate authorities can issue certificates for IP addresses, not just domain names. It defines a new identifier type for IP addresses and a challenge that lets a client show it controls the address in question.

plainLanguage.summary: ACME originally checked whether an applicant controlled a domain name. This RFC adds a way to request certificates for an IP address and defines how two existing challenges can validate that address.

questions: how to get a certificate for an ip address
does acme support ip address identifiers
which acme challenges work for ip addresses
how does acme validate an ip address
which acme challenges support ip identifiers
can dns-01 validate an ip identifier
subtitle: ACME can validate control of IP addresses for certificate requests.

tldr.problem: ACME originally defined challenges for DNS host names, not for IP address identifiers.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC adds the ip identifier and permits http-01 and tls-alpn-01 validation without DNS resolution. The dns-01 challenge MUST NOT be used for IP identifiers.
tldr.outcome: An ACME server can validate control of IPv4 or IPv6 identifiers for certificates.

today: RFC 8738 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The IP Identifier
sections.content:
RFC 8555 defines the DNS identifier type. To ask a user to prove control of an IPv4 or IPv6 address, an ACME server MUST create an authorization with identifier type ip.

The value is the address in its required textual form. The RFC gives {"type": "ip", "value": "2001:db8::1"} as an IPv6 example.
sections.plainLanguage: An authorization can identify an IP address instead of a domain name. The address is written in the standard text form for IPv4 or IPv6.

sections.title: Validating an IP Address
sections.content:
IP identifiers MAY use the http-01 or tls-alpn-01 challenge. Both MUST skip the initial DNS lookup and use the identifier's IP address for validation.

For http-01, the Host header MUST contain that address. For tls-alpn-01, the validation certificate MUST contain one matching iPAddress in subjectAltName; the SNI HostName uses the address's IN-ADDR.ARPA or IP6.ARPA reverse mapping, because SNI does not permit IP addresses there. The dns-01 challenge MUST NOT validate an IP identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: The two allowed checks connect to the address itself rather than looking up a domain name. DNS-based dns-01 is not allowed for an IP identifier.

sections.title: ACME Registry Entries
sections.content: IANA added the ip label to the ACME Identifier Types registry. It also added validation-method entries for http-01 and tls-alpn-01 with identifier type ip.
sections.plainLanguage: The ACME registries now list ip as an identifier type and record which two validation methods support it.

sections.title: Security and Certificate Authority Policy
sections.content:
The extensions do not deviate from the threat model in RFC 8555. The RFC explains how a server may check that an applicant controls an IP identifier at validation time.

A certificate authority may choose additional checks. The RFC gives short IP delegation periods at an ISP or cloud provider as a reason a CA might restrict certificates.
sections.plainLanguage: The check shows control of the address at the time of validation. A certificate authority may add checks if an address could soon be assigned to someone else.
